Completely remove the bolt securing the pedal to the shaft (B, Figure 96).
Before removing the pedal, note how the spring contacts the post on the brake stay and pedal.
Hold the pedal shaft in place, then pull the pedal from the shaft.
Remove the pedal shaft and spring.
Clean and inspect the parts.
Inspect the pedal shaft and bore bushing for scoring, damage or the entry of water and dirt. If the bushing is worn, replace it.
Inspect the clevis pin and pedal bore. The pin must be a firm fit in the clevis and pedal.
Inspect the spring and shaft bolt for corrosion and damage.
Check that the brake stay is tightly fastened.
Install the pedal as follows:
Apply waterproof grease to the bushing and pedal shaft.
Install the spring, seating it against the brake stay. The straight end of the spring rests against the back of the brake stay post.
Install the pedal shaft. Engage the hooked end of the spring with the narrow arm on the pedal shaft.
Hold the shaft in place, then turn it forward to preload the spring.
Install the pedal, guiding it into the clevis, and aligning the index marks on the pedal and shaft (C, Figure 96).
Bolt the pedal to the shaft.
For proper brake pedal height, check that the pushrod threads protrude 3-3.5 mm (0.12-0.14 in.) below the nut in the clevis (Figure 93). Adjust the clevis position if necessary.
Install the clevis pin and a new cotter pin.
Attach the brake light switch spring.
Check pedal height and operation. If the pedal is not level with the footpeg, inspect for bent or damaged parts.
Check brake light operation. If necessary, adjust the switch (Chapter Three).

To drain the brake fluid from the system, have a 10 mm wrench, tip-resistant container and a length of clear tubing that fits snugly on the bleeder valve. Use the following procedure to drain either the front or rear brakes.
Brake fluid can damage painted and finished surfaces. Use water to immediately wash any surface that becomes contaminated with brake fluid.
Attach one end of the tubing to the bleeder valve and place the other end into the container (Figure 97).
Open the bleeder valve so fluid can pass into the tubing.
Pump the brake lever/pedal to force the fluid from the system.
When the system no longer drips fluid, close the bleeder valve.
Dispose the brake fluid in an environmentally safe manner.

Whenever the brake fluid is replaced, or if the brake lever or pedal feels spongy, bleed the brakes to purge all air from the system. Before bleeding the brakes, determine where the air is entering the system. Check all brake components for leakage, and fittings and hoses for deterioration, damage or looseness. The brake system can be bled manually or by using a vacuum pump. Both methods are described in this section.
Before bleeding brakes, always secure the bike so it is stable and locked in place, particularly the fork. This minimizes the chance of spilled fluid jrom an open reservoir.
Brake Fluid Reservoirs

Regardless of the bleeding method used, the reservoir cap of the master cylinder being bled must be removed so the reservoir can be filled with brake fluid. The reservoirs must not be over or under filled. Note the following when working with each reservoir.
Front brake reservoir.
After removing the cap, remove the diaphragm from the reservoir before filling with fluid.
Keep the reservoir filled between the top of the sight glass and the lower mark on the reservoir (Figure 98) during the bleeding procedure.
After bleeding, replenish the reservoir to the upper mark, then install the diaphragm and cap.
Rear brake reservoir.
Remove the reservoir guard and backing plate. Remove the cap, diaphragm plate and diaphragm.
Keep the reservoir filled between the upper and lower marks on the reservoir during the bleeding procedure (Figure 99).
After bleeding, replenish the reservoir to the upper mark, then install the diaphragm, diaphragm plate and cap.
Install the backing plate and reservoir guard.
Manual Bleeding

To manually bleed the brake system, have a 10 mm wrench, tip-resistant container and a length of clear tubing that fits snugly on the brake bleeder. Bleeding the system is much easier if two people are available to perform the procedure. One person can open and close the bleeder valve while the other person operates the brake lever or pedal. Use the following procedure to bleed either the front or rear brake.
Brake fluid can damage painted and finished surfaces. Use water and immediately wash any surface that becomes contaminated with brake fluid.
Attach one end of the tubing to the bleeder valve and place the other end into the container (Figure 97).
Fill the reservoir to the upper level with DOT 4 brake fluid.
Do not use brake fluid from an unsealed container. It will have absorbed moisture from the air and already be contaminated. Use DOT 4 brake fluid from a sealed container.

Apply pressure (do not pump) to the brake lever or pedal, then open the bleeder valve. As the fluid is forced from the system, the lever/pedal travels its full length of operation. When the lever/pedal can move no farther, hold the lever/pedal in the down position and close the bleeder valve. Do not allow the lever or pedal to return to its up position before the bleeder valve is closed. Air will be drawn into the system.
In the following step, release the lever/pedal slowly. This minimizes the chance of fluid splashing out of the reservoir, as excess fluid in the brake line is returned to the reservoir.
When the bleeder valve is closed, release the lever/pedal so it returns to its up position. Check the
fluid level in the reservoir and replenish, if necessary.

During the bleeding process, the reservoir must contain fluid during the entire procedure. If the reservoir is allowed to become empty, air will be in the system and the bleeding process will have to be repeated.

Repeat Step 3 and Step 4 until clear fluid (minimal air bubbles) is seen passing out of the bleeder valve. Unless the bleeder valve threads are wrapped with Teflon tape, or coated with silicone brake grease, a small amount of air will enter the system when the bleeder valve is opened.

If small bubbles (foam) remain in the system after several bleeding attempts, close the reservoir and allow the system to stand undisturbed for a few hours. The system will stabilize and the air can be purged as large bubbles.
The bleeding procedure is completed when the feel of the lever/pedal is firm.
Check the brake fluid reservoir and fill the reservoir to the upper level, if necessary.
Tighten the bleeder valve to 8 N•m (70 in.-lb.). Do not overtighten.
Dispose the waste brake fluid in an environmentally safe manner.
Vacuum Bleeding
To vacuum-bleed the brake system, have a 10 mm wrench and a vacuum pump, such as the Mityvac pump shown in Figure 100. Use the following procedure to bleed either the front or rear brake.
Brake fluid can damage painted and finished surfaces. Use water and immediately wash any surface that becomes contaminated with brake fluid.
Check that the banjo bolts are tight at the master cylinder and caliper.
Attach the brake bleeder to the bleeder valve (Figure 100). Suspend the tool with wire. This al-
lows the tool to be released when the fluid reservoir needs to be refilled.
Fill the reservoir to the upper level with DOT 4 brake fluid.
Do not use brake fluid from an unsealed container. It will have absorbed moisture from the air and already be contaminated. Use DOT 4 brake fluid from a sealed container.

During the bleeding process, the reservoir must contain fluid during the entire procedure. If the reservoir is allowed to become empty, air will be in the system and the bleeding process will have to be repeated.
Pump the handle on the brake bleeder to create a vacuum.

Open the bleeder valve and draw the air and fluid from the system. Close the valve before the fluid stops moving. If the vacuum pump is equipped with a gauge, close the bleeder before the gauge reads 0 in. Hg. Replenish the fluid level in the reservoir.

Repeat Step 4 and Step 5 until clear fluid (minimal air bubbles) is passing out of the bleeder. Unless the bleeder valve threads are wrapped with Teflon tape, or coated with silicone brake grease, a small amount of air will enter the system when the bleeder valve is opened. The bleeding procedure is completed when the feel of the lever/pedal is firm.
Check the brake fluid reservoir and fill the reservoir to the upper level, if necessary.
Tighten the bleeder valve to 8 N•m (70 in.-lb.). Do not overtighten.
Dispose the waste brake fluid in an environmentally safe manner.

The condition of the brake discs and pads are often a reflection of one another. If disc scoring is evident, inspect the pads and disc as soon as possible. Visually inspect the discs and pads with the wheels mounted on the motorcycle (Chapter Three). If damage is detected, perform the inspections described in this section.

Do not true a deeply scored or warped disc. Removing disc material causes the disc to overheat rapidly and warp. Maintain the discs by keeping them clean and corrosion-free. Use a solvent, that is not oil-based, to wipe grit that accumulates on the discs and at the edge of the pads.
Thickness and Runout Inspection
Measure the thickness of each disc at several locations around its perimeter (Figure 101). Refer to Table 1 for the service limit. Replace the disc if it is out of specification.
Measure disc runout as follows:
Mount a dial indicator on a stable surface and in contact with the disc (Figure 102).
Zero the gauge.
Turn the wheel and watch the amount of runout measured on the gauge.
Refer to Table 1 for the service limit. Replace the disc if it is out of specification.

If the disc runout is out of specification, check the condition of the wheel bearings before replacing the disc. If the bearings are not in good condition, the bearings should be replaced before disc runout is determined.
Removal and Installation
The discs are mounted to the hubs with bolts. Remove and install either disc as follows:
Remove the wheel from motorcycle (Chapter Eleven).
Remove the bolts (Figure 103) that secure the disc to the hub.

This chapter provides removal and installation procedures for the side covers, seat, fuel tank, radiator covers, skid plate, front fender, fairing and subframe. When removing or installing the bodywork, do not use excessive force. Although the bodywork is flexible, it will discolor when it is excessively flexed or pinched.
Removal and Installation
Remove the screws at the front and rear of the cover (Figure 1).
Pull the bottom of the cover out to remove the friction barb from the grommet.
Remove the cover.
To install the cover:
Insert the rear edge of the cover first. The cover must fit under the rear fender.
Align the friction barb with the grommet, then press the cover into place.
Install and tighten the screws.
Removal and Installation
Remove the side covers as described in this chapter.
Remove the bolt (Figure 2) from both sides of the seat.
Grasp the front and rear of the seat, then pull it backwards to disengage it from the fuel tank (Figure 3).
Reverse this procedure to install the seat. Check that the seat is secure at the front.
Removal and Installation
Remove the seat as described in this chapter.
Turn the fuel valve off.
Remove the fuel hose (A, Figure 4) and vacuum hose (B) from the fuel valve assembly.
Remove the bolts and hose(s) at the rear of the fuel tank (Figure 5).
Remove the screw at the top of the radiator cover (Figure 6), then pull the friction barb from the grommet in the fuel tank. Do not excessively flex the cover.
Remove the fuel tank, moving it toward the rear of the motorcycle.
Reverse this procedure to install the fuel tank. Align the fuel tank with all bolt and screw holes before tightening the fasteners.

At the left side of the motorcycle, the cover shrouds the radiator. At the right side, the cover shrouds the coolant reserve tank. If desired, the coyers can be removed with the fuel tank. Only the fasteners at the front of the covers need to be removed. If the covers remain attached to the fuel tank, support the fuel tank after removal, so it does not rest on the flexible covers.

At the front of the cover, remove the bolt/screw at the top and bottom of the cover (Figure 7).
Remove the screw at the top of the radiator cover, then pull the friction barb from the grommet
in the fuel tank (Figure 6). Do not excessively flex the cover.
Reverse this procedure to install the radiator covers.

The skid plate is attached to the frame by three bolts and collars (Figure 8). If using the motorcycle in rough terrain, inspect the skid plate often. Consider a metal aftermarket skid plate when operating the motorcycle in rough conditions.
The front fender is attached to the fork by four bolts and washers (Figure 9).

Cover the front fender or remove the fender.
Remove the upper mounting bolt from the frame (Figure 10). If necessary, loosen the lower bolt so the fairing can be tilted forward.
Tilt the fairing forward and remove the wire ties securing the wiring to the framework.

Disconnect the turn signal wires and unplug the headlight. Keep the turn signal wires identified. Also, remove the wires from the frame tab. the lower mounting bolt from the 5. Remove frame. Support the fairing while removing the bolt.
Inspect the fairing and frame for damage.
Reverse this procedure to install the fairing. Clean all electrical connections, then lightly apply dielectric grease to the connectors.

Remove the side covers and seat as described in this chapter.
Remove the muffler from the exhaust pipe and frame (Chapter Four).
Remove the right passenger footpeg (A, Figure 11).
Loosen the carburetor clamp (A, Figure 12).
Remove the battery (Chapter Three).
Disconnect all hoses and wires passing from the front to the rear of the motorcycle (Figure 13). Route the hoses and wires out of the subframe.
